prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of GLP-1 and the identification of its active form, which made incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: The round-1 exchange did not change my configuration, and I note that the unanimity on B012 is not what carries it. The case rests on a discovery with a clear change in two fields: Holst's physiology of GLP-1 secretion and incretin action, Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, and Drucker's proglucagon-derived peptide biology and its metabolic and intestinotropic actions. These came before any long-acting agonist and made one possible. The result has been confirmed independently in large randomized outcome trials for glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal disease, so there is no question of waiting for impact to appear. The three-person ceiling forces a choice, and honouring the discoveries of mechanism and active peptide is the defensible reading of a prize for a discovery and not for a product. A single-part prize with a citation that names the physiology and the active form keeps the credit within what these three can fairly claim.
statement.case_against: Two weaknesses remain and round 2 did not remove either. First, the credit: Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested relative to Habener and colleagues, who are not on the supplied list, and I cannot settle that from the files. Second, leaving out Lotte Bjerre Knudsen means the prize does not reward the protraction chemistry that turned a peptide with a half-life of minutes into a medicine, which Svenningsson and Linnarsson rightly say is more than routine translation. The citation therefore has to say what it rewards and not imply more. If the committee decided the therapeutic step is what should be recognised, my trio would be the wrong one, though I would not accept swapping Knudsen in at the expense of the physiology names without a new argument. The obesity indication and long-term safety data are also still evolving, but I do not regard that as a maturity problem.

responses.point: Linnarsson accepts the trio but says the question is not closed, because native GLP-1 has a half-life of minutes and the protraction chemistry is more than routine translation, so the citation must say openly that it does not capture drug engineering.
responses.response: I accept this and have changed my citation accordingly. It now names the physiology and the active form and says these made the therapies possible, so it does not claim the prize rewards the agonists. I still hold that excluding Knudsen is defensible, because the prize recognises a discovery and the mechanism and peptide identity were in place before any long-acting agonist existed. I do not agree that the exclusion can be hidden. A citation that says the discoveries enabled the therapies states the boundary honestly. I would not reopen it unless the committee concluded that the engineering was itself the decisive scientific step. On the evidence in the files I do not think it was.

responses.point: Sandberg says excluding Knudsen is defensible, but that making a peptide with a half-life of days was a scientific achievement, and that if Mojsov's priority proves weaker than it appears the case for Knudsen becomes strong.
responses.response: That conditional is the right test and I agree with its form. If the committee could establish that Mojsov's identification of the active peptide was not independent or not first, the third name would have to be reconsidered, and Knudsen would be one candidate, though Habener would be another. We cannot settle it here, so my position is that a configuration with Mojsov is defensible on the record we have, because her synthesis and characterisation of GLP-1(7-36) is documented as a distinct contribution. I would disclose the uncertainty rather than treat it as resolved. Where I differ is in the fallback. A priority problem is a reason to look again at the basic-science names, not automatically to move to the drug developers.

responses.point: The chair says the clean attribution of B024 is a reason for comfort and not a measure of merit, that Ron and the PERK arm are a real limit I played down, and that B024 should not rank ahead of the clinical candidates.
responses.response: I accept both points in part. I argued in round 1 that the Walter and Mori pair is clean, and clean credit is not merit. The merit is the mechanism: the unfolded protein response is a conceptually deep, thoroughly confirmed signalling pathway that changed how the field thinks about endoplasmic reticulum stress. I also accept that the omission of the PERK arm and Ron is a real limit and that I had understated it. I agree it should not outrank the clinical case this year, and in my final ballot B024 is an alternative and not a co-equal second part. The three-person ceiling also settles the matter, because B012 already uses three names and no second part can be added. I keep B024 as my first alternative because its science is mature even though translation is early.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius asks whether excluding Knudsen is defensible or merely convenient, and wants the citation worded so it does not overstate what the three basic scientists achieved.
responses.response: I think it is defensible and not merely convenient, for the reason she gives: the discoveries about incretin physiology and the active peptide precede and enable the pharmaceutical engineering. The convenience argument does apply to the three-person cap, and I do not want to rely on it. I would rest the exclusion on the criterion and not on the ceiling. I agree on the wording and have narrowed it to physiology and the identification of the active form, with the therapies described as made possible by them, not as the thing being rewarded. I also take her warning that a foregone conclusion invites a lighter test. That is why I re-examined the attribution weaknesses and found them real but not enough to change the configuration.

responses.point: El-Manira asks whether the deciding step for TNF blockade (B046) was showing that TNF drives synovial inflammation or clinical proof of concept, and says that if it is the first he would raise it.
responses.response: I think the answer bears on whether B046 is a discovery prize at all. Feldmann and Maini's argument that TNF is a dominant driver in the rheumatoid synovium was a distinctive and testable hypothesis, so there is a real mechanistic claim. But the target biology, the antibodies and the fusion proteins have many other contributors, and the clinical proof of concept is what made the case convincing. I do not think this resolves enough to place B046 as a second part this year. It remains a strong candidate for a later year, and it is not in my alternatives only because B024 and B009 are more mature as discoveries.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for identifying the active GLP-1 peptide can be established relative to Habener and colleagues, who are not on the supplied credit list.
Whether the committee would accept a citation that openly limits the prize to physiology and the active form, with the long-acting agonist engineering by Knudsen and others left unrewarded.

Whether the second part question is moot: with three names on B012 and a three-person ceiling, no second distinct achievement can be added, so the choice is a single GLP-1 prize or a different structure altogether.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level conflict is apparent for the shortlisted candidates. I disclose approximately twenty co-authored works with Per Svenningsson, one 2009 paper with Abdel El Manira, a prior Salk-period collaboration with Ronald Evans, and collaboration with Johan Ericson at KI. None of these is a credited name on the shortlist. This is unchanged from round 1, and I flag it only as disclosure.
